title: Bluetooth discovery and transactions
text:
# Bluetooth discovery and transactions

These commands use the shared HTTP, WebSocket, MCP, HTML and Lua executor. Android Bluetooth access and an enabled adapter are required. Android 12 and later distinguish scan and connect access; older scans require location access. Requests do not silently enable the radio or bypass peripheral security.

title: Bluetooth discovery and transactions: Discover and pair
text:
## Discover and pair

`bluetoothScan` / `dikciz_bluetooth_scan` selects `mode: ble` or `classic`. `durationMilliseconds` defaults to 5000, range 1 through 120000. `maximumDevices` defaults to 50, range 1 through 200. Results report actual discovered addresses, nullable names, types, bond state and RSSI, plus count and whether the device limit was reached. A scan owns only its own discovery and releases it after completion. Classic discovery refuses to interrupt an existing scan.

`bluetoothPair` / `dikciz_bluetooth_pair` takes an explicit `address`. Already bonded devices report paired. A newly accepted bond request reports submitted, not completed pairing; Android may show owner confirmation. Check `bluetoothDevices` afterward.

title: Bluetooth discovery and transactions: Classic RFCOMM
text:
## Classic RFCOMM

`bluetoothExchange` / `dikciz_bluetooth_exchange` requires `address` and canonical `serviceUuid`. `secure` defaults to true. Optional `dataBase64` writes at most 65536 decoded bytes. `readBytes` defaults to 4096, range 0 through 65536, and reads one available chunk. It does not promise a complete application message. Results report actual byte counts, Base64 input and end-of-stream state.

`timeoutMilliseconds` defaults to 30000, range 1 through 120000. A deadline closes the owned socket and frees the connection slot. A failure may follow partial output. Use the peer's protocol to confirm an operation before retrying.

title: Bluetooth discovery and transactions: BLE GATT
text:
## BLE GATT

`bluetoothGatt` / `dikciz_bluetooth_gatt` opens one owned connection for one action, then disconnects and closes it. Required fields are `address` and `action`. Actions:

| Action | Selection and result |
| --- | --- |
| `discover` | Optional serviceUuid filter; offset/limit pagination over service, characteristic and descriptor records. Results include properties, permissions and instance IDs. |
| `read`, `write` | serviceUuid and characteristicUuid; writes require dataBase64. |
| `readDescriptor`, `writeDescriptor` | Service and characteristic UUIDs plus descriptorUuid; writes require dataBase64. |
| `observe` | Service and characteristic UUIDs; enables its CCCD and collects at most maximumEvents, default 1 and maximum 100. |

All UUIDs use canonical hyphenated form. Duplicate UUIDs require discovered `serviceInstanceId` or `characteristicInstanceId`. Writes are bounded to 512 decoded bytes. Characteristic `writeType` is default, noResponse or signed. An accepted no-response write cannot prove the peer applied it.

Optional `mtu` is 23 through 517; the result reports the negotiated value when Android supplies it. The shared timeout defaults to 30000 ms, maximum 120000. Observation timeout after subscription returns the collected events with `windowExpired: true`; connection or subscription failure remains an error. Each event contains actual bytes and its timestamp. Connections are not retained between commands.

title: Bluetooth discovery and transactions: Example
text:
## Example

```json
{"type":"bluetoothScan","mode":"ble","durationMilliseconds":5000}
```

Discovery can return no devices. Successful GATT/RFCOMM exchange needs a compatible external peer. See [hardware inventories](hardware-controls.md), [USB](usb-control.md) and [command schemas](command-reference.md).

title: Bluetooth discovery and transactions: Companion workflows
text:
## Companion workflows

See [the focused companion guide](device-connections.md) for the new shared commands, native screens, required access and actual outcome states.

title: Camera capture controls
text:
# Camera capture controls

Use `cameraList`, then `cameraCapabilities` for the selected `cameraId`. Ordinary HTTP, WebSocket, MCP, HTML and Lua use the same `cameraCapture` command. Camera access and Android foreground eligibility are required. Missing access uses the common permission-review flow; explicitly retry after the owner grants it.

title: Camera capture controls: Request
text:
## Request

| Field | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `cameraId` | Camera inventory ID. Defaults to the first camera. |
| `maxDimension` | Largest allowed JPEG dimension, 320 through 4096, default 1280. The largest supported fitting size wins. |
| `timeoutMilliseconds` | Overall capture wait, 1 through 120000, default 30000. |
| `jpegQuality` | JPEG quality, 1 through 100, default 95. |
| `jpegOrientation` | Optional 0, 90, 180 or 270 degrees. Android may rotate pixels or encode EXIF orientation. |
| `zoomPercent` | Optional centered sensor crop, 100 through 10000, bounded by `maximumDigitalZoom × 100` for this camera. It does not select another physical lens. |
| `exposureCompensation` | Optional integer steps within the camera's reported range. Multiply by `exposureCompensationStepEv` to obtain EV. |
| `autofocusMode` | Optional Android mode from `autofocusModes`: 0 off, 1 auto, 2 macro, 3 continuous video, 4 continuous picture, 5 extended depth of field. |

~~~json
{"type":"cameraCapture","cameraId":"0","jpegQuality":90,"jpegOrientation":90,"zoomPercent":150}
~~~

Select the camera and zoom from actual discovery rather than assuming that this example ID or zoom exists. Unspecified focus, orientation, exposure and zoom retain the still-capture template defaults. The command makes one still request; it does not run a preview or a separate autofocus/exposure convergence sequence.

title: Camera capture controls: Result and files
text:
## Result and files

Success requires both written JPEG bytes and Android's completed capture callback. The result includes `state:saved`, generated `path`, `mimeType:image/jpeg`, `bytes`, `cameraId`, configured output `width` and `height`, `requestedControls` and `captureMetadata`.

Requested controls describe the submitted settings. Metadata contains Android's actual frame number, sensor timestamp, JPEG quality/orientation, exposure compensation, autofocus mode/state, auto-exposure state and crop rectangle. Missing result fields are JSON null. Sensor timestamps are monotonic camera timestamps, not UTC. Requested values do not prove focus convergence, exposure quality or physical scene contents. Android can adjust a requested crop to match output aspect ratios.

Read or download the file through the ordinary file APIs, then remove it when finished. Capture filenames are generated under app-specific external capture storage. No caller output path is accepted. Width and height describe the configured camera output; clients must honor JPEG/EXIF orientation when displaying it.

Unsupported device ranges or modes return `camera_control_unsupported` before opening the camera. Invalid types and generic bounds return `validation_failed`. Busy, disconnected, configuration, image-write, capture and deadline failures are explicit. Failed or timed-out requests close the session/device/reader and remove incomplete files. Late open callbacks close their device before releasing ownership. A client disconnect does not prove capture cancellation; inspect a durable command job when reconnectable results are needed.

For persistent camera preview and Accessibility display JPEGs, use [live image streams](visual-streams.md). Managed multi-command video recording remains separate.

title: Camera capture controls: Bounded video
text:
## Bounded video

`cameraVideoRecord` / `dikciz_camera_video_record` saves foreground H.264 video in an MP4 container. Discover `videoSizes` and `frameRateRanges` through `cameraCapabilities` first. Size/rate/encoder combinations can still be rejected by Android.

| Field | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `cameraId` | Defaults to the first discovered camera. |
| `durationMilliseconds` | 1000 through 120000, default 3000. |
| `timeoutMilliseconds` | 1 through 300000, default 30000. Must cover duration and allow camera startup. |
| `maxDimension` | 320 through 1920, default 1280. Largest fitting recorder size wins. |
| `frameRate` | 5 through 60, default 30. Chooses the narrowest advertised camera range containing it. |
| `bitRate` | H.264 bits per second, 500000 through 20000000, default 4000000. |
| `orientation` | MP4 playback hint 0, 90, 180 or 270, default 0. Source pixels are not rotated. |
| `withAudio` | Default false. True additionally requires and owns microphone access, recording mono AAC. |

Photo and video requests share camera ownership. Audio-enabled video shares microphone ownership with the existing recording and recognition APIs. Competing requests return `hardware_busy`. Android foreground loss, camera/recorder errors and deadlines fail the operation and discard incomplete files.

Success requires recorder finalization, completed camera frames and Android media inspection. Results include the saved path, `mimeType:video/mp4`, bytes, actual `durationMilliseconds`, dimensions, rotation and `hasAudio`. Requested duration/frame rate and the chosen camera FPS range remain separate from observed metadata. `observedCaptureFrames` counts camera callbacks, not encoded output frames.

Read/download the completed file through ordinary file APIs and remove it when finished. Native startup and recording checks respect the overall deadline; blocking platform stop/cleanup calls may take additional time. A finalized container proves encoded media exists, not physical image or sound quality. This bounded video command has no caller output path or background recording service. JPEG preview uses the separate image-stream commands.

Use [durable jobs](command-jobs.md) for reconnectable results. Cancel requests interruption; poll status and confirm cleanup before replacement work. In-process calls from HTML and Lua use the same command, permissions and result. Lua's native host request time is excluded from its script execution budget.

title: Capability coverage
text:
# Capability coverage

This table describes dedicated Dikciz operations. Generic intents, shell and Accessibility can cover additional tasks, but do not turn them into a typed API. The installed build's discovery is authoritative. New commands in this working version are not present in older APKs.

| Area | Implemented | Remaining |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Launcher | Pages, grid, widgets, shortcuts/groups, themes, editing and full configuration | Continued platform compatibility and focused UI improvements. |
| Custom apps | Complete editable HTML/CSS/JS and Lua/JS bundles, independent state/files, shared Dikciz command access, native/custom subscriptions, persistent timers, urgent modals and source-only archives; bundled SOS, Voice notes, Agenda, Device status and the GPS Travel todo reference | Separate APK identities and inclusion in encrypted home/chat backups are not implemented. See [custom apps](custom-apps.md). |
| On-device assistant | OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible streaming providers, native Markdown chat, SQLite conversations, encrypted keys, context trimming/summarization, shared MCP tools/event rules and five enforced read-only routines | Additional provider wire protocols and exact per-model tokenizers. |
| Offline search | Persistent SQLite collections, weighted ranking, prefixes, reviewed aliases, typo correction, full-text reads, live schemas and trusted read-only filtering across every ordinary binding | Semantic embeddings, automatic translation and automatic private-data crawling are not implemented. |
| Recovery and operations | Persistent metadata timeline, scoped resource measurements and pause controls, visual Lua rule testing, encrypted home/chat backup with preview and rollback recovery | Per-widget battery attribution is unavailable from ordinary Android APIs. |
| Shared control | Ordinary HTTP, WebSocket, MCP, HTML and Lua commands; validation, Android permission review and incremental shell sessions and replayable event reads | Additional native stream formats and general push delivery for scripts. |
| Speech input | Provider discovery, strict on-device/system modes, language, bounded recognition, alternatives/confidence, partial-result cursor streams, explicit recorded-file provider transcription, cancellation, provider language inventory and observed model-download requests | Provider-dependent partial support and additional transcription wire protocols. |
| Speech output | Device text-to-speech, voice inventory, voice/language/rate/pitch selection, completion/errors, saved WAV synthesis and explicit stop | Engine-specific advanced synthesis features. |
| Audio | Bounded and managed microphone recording with input preference, foreground-service PCM streaming with cursor replay and owner stop, device inventory, local playback sessions with pause/resume/seek, volume, focus and preferred output | Live audio output and additional recording formats. |
| Camera | Camera inventory, JPEG controls/actual frame metadata, bounded foreground H.264 MP4 with optional AAC, persistent JPEG preview streams and capability discovery | Managed multi-command video recording sessions. |
| Sensors | Static/dynamic inventory, bounded readings, background subscriptions, live starter page and SQLite dispatch replay and acknowledged consumers | Raw sample replay before bus coalescing. |
| Location | Bounded current fix/cache, accuracy/age/source, optional place name, background subscriptions, weather integration, geocoding/GNSS status, accuracy-aware geofences and recorded routes | Raw GNSS diagnostics. Dedicated geofences and route history are described in [journeys](safety-and-journeys.md). |

title: Capability coverage: Platform-restricted work
text:
## Platform-restricted work

Cellular call-stream recording and injection need privileged system integration. Silent permission grants, arbitrary private app data and protected system settings are not ordinary app capabilities. Owner-enabled Accessibility, special access, a device-owner deployment or root can change specific capabilities, but none grants every Android API automatically. Fastboot/bootloader control is outside a running Android app.

Screen recording through MediaProjection needs the platform consent flow. Camera and microphone have foreground and privacy restrictions. Bluetooth/Wi-Fi/NFC/USB availability depends on hardware and Android access. A missing device is an explicit result, not a reason to report simulated success.

title: Durable command jobs
text:
# Durable command jobs

`jobStart`, `jobStatus`, `jobsList` and `jobCancel` share the ordinary command dispatcher across HTTP, WebSocket, MCP, HTML and Lua. Use them when a request should continue after its transport disconnects. Shell streaming remains a connection-owned stream and is not a job.

title: Durable command jobs: Submit and retrieve
text:
## Submit and retrieve

Submit a full ordinary command and a unique `idempotencyKey`:

```json
{"type":"jobStart","idempotencyKey":"example-sample-1","command":{"type":"sensorReadings","timeoutMilliseconds":1000}}
```

The response gives `jobId`, `state`, creation/expiry times, cancellation state and `deduplicated`. An identical key and command return the same job. Changed content returns `job_idempotency_conflict`. Retention is part of the original submission; reusing the key does not extend it. Set `retentionHours` from 1 to 720; default 168 hours. There are at most 256 retained jobs and two concurrent workers. Expired terminal records are removed when a job command runs. Full capacity returns `job_capacity`.

Use `jobStatus` with `jobId`. Its `response` preserves the original ordinary command envelope, including result data, errors and permission recovery. `jobsList` accepts `limit` 1 through 200, default 50, and nonnegative `offset` up to 1000000. It returns metadata, `total` and `hasMore`, newest first. Results are omitted from the list. Follow the returned count and fetch each needed result separately.

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `queued` | Persisted and waiting for a worker. |
| `running` | The shared dispatcher is executing the command. |
| `completed` | The original command returned a result envelope. Inspect that result to determine its actual effect. |
| `failed` | The original command returned an error, or job execution/storage failed. |
| `cancelled` | Queued work was cancelled before execution. |
| `interrupted` | A previous process stopped before recording a final outcome. Work is not replayed. |

`outcomeKnown` is false when process loss or an unexpected execution failure leaves the effect unknown. A completed command can itself report unavailable, submitted, pending or permission-required state. Job completion does not strengthen that claim.

title: Durable command jobs: Cancellation and recovery
text:
## Cancellation and recovery

`jobCancel` cancels queued work or requests interruption of a running worker. `cancellationRequested` remains visible. Android operations may already have caused effects, may ignore interruption or may finish concurrently. A cancellation request never rolls back effects. Poll the final result before deciding whether to retry.

Records survive transport disconnects, launcher recreation and process restart. On startup, retained queued/running work becomes `interrupted` with unknown outcome. Automatic replay would duplicate non-idempotent actions, so the caller must inspect the external effect and explicitly submit any replacement work.

Job commands cannot enqueue other job commands or mutate remote authentication. Arguments and results are kept in app-private storage and excluded from operation logs. Requests still use the existing authentication and safe-mode rules. Permissions are checked when work executes. Set `autoRequestPermissions` on the nested command, or inherit it from `jobStart`, to request owner review. Granting permission does not retry a failed job automatically.

MCP tools: `dikciz_job_start`, `dikciz_job_status`, `dikciz_jobs_list`, `dikciz_job_cancel`. HTML uses `dikciz.command`; Lua uses its ordinary Android-command bridge. Read [command discovery](automation-control.md), [permissions](native-device-control.md) and [coverage](capability-coverage.md).

Malformed or oversized retained records fail job initialization with `job_storage_invalid`. Repeated calls keep failing rather than exposing a partial record set. Removing or repairing the damaged app-private record allows a later initialization attempt; this does not replay interrupted work.

title: Safety, journeys and devices
text:
# Safety, journeys and devices

Open **Settings**, **Safety, journeys and devices**. Each tab uses the shared command executor, Android access checks and ordinary response contracts. Launcher controls display the installed version beside Close.

The Safety tab opens the bundled SOS [custom app](custom-apps.md). Its complete UI and backend are editable under `/sdcard/Dikciz/apps/sos/`. **Dikciz**, **Apps** also includes Voice notes, Agenda, Device status and Travel todo, plus creation, complete-source editing and import/export. Places, Trips and the remaining companion tabs keep their native controls.

| Task | Guide |
| --- | --- |
| Choose contacts, preview messages, arm a missed check-in or record a route | [Safety and journeys](safety-and-journeys.md) |
| Keep a Bluetooth, USB or NFC connection across commands | [Device connections and Vehicle console](device-connections.md) |
| Read text/barcodes or create cleaned image PDFs | [Image recognition](image-recognition.md) |
| Inspect grants, read/aggregate records and write owned Health Connect data | [Health records](health-records.md) |
| Suggest/save a network, request a local connection or start a local-only hotspot | [Wi-Fi networks](wifi-networks.md) |
| Run repeatable read-only briefings with a saved provider | [Assistant routines](assistant-routines.md) |
| Stage base/split APKs together or cancel an owned install session | [Package installation](package-installation.md) |

MCP starts at dikciz://docs/guides/companion. Search also indexes the focused manuals and installed tool schemas. Missing hardware, provider access or foreground eligibility remains explicit. Nothing starts sending SMS, recording a route or connecting a peripheral merely because the app was installed.

Companion commands currently require full owner remote authority. Scoped tokens retain their existing finite grants and cannot use these commands to acquire broader access. Assistant read-only enforcement remains independent.

title: Safety, journeys and devices: Native controls
text:
## Native controls

These captures show the isolated emulator, including a fictional safety contact. They demonstrate setup controls, not carrier delivery or physical-peripheral compatibility.

title: Custom apps
text:
# Custom apps

Open **Dikciz**, **Apps** to open, create, edit, enable, disable, export or remove a complete app. Each app combines its own HTML/CSS/JavaScript interface with a Lua or headless JavaScript backend and persistent state. Closing its WebView leaves subscribed events and scheduled backend work available through the native host.

These are apps inside Dikciz. Android does not install a separate APK or grant them separate Android identities. Every app inherits the Android access granted to Dikciz, including its phone commands, files, shell and SDK access. There is no separate app permission screen, command allowlist or manifest approval. Android still enforces the permissions and special access granted to the Dikciz package.

title: Custom apps: Bundled apps
text:
## Bundled apps

| App | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Travel todo | Editable checklist with an opt-in GPS arrival rule and a custom-event input. Follow the [complete tutorial](todo-app-tutorial.md). |
| SOS check-ins | Editable contact plans, preview, explicit arming, cancellation countdown, tracked SMS and periodic location updates. All workflow decisions live in `apps/sos/main.js`; the UI lives beside it. |
| Voice notes | Record, save and replay local audio. Recording begins on a tap and stops when the app is hidden. Saved files belong to this app. |
| Agenda and alarms | Upcoming calendar entries, next Android alarm and links to Android calendar/alarm apps. Calendar access is optional and requested explicitly. |
| Device status | Live battery, memory, storage, process CPU history and Android-exposed per-core data. Restricted system counters remain explicit. |

Bundled source installs only when absent. Updates preserve customized bundles. Removing a bundled app records that choice, so reopening Home does not silently reinstall it. Voice notes, Agenda and Device status reuse the complete widget documents as independent apps; their UI polling stops when hidden. SOS uses its backend for deadlines and outgoing effects. Geofences, route capture and the visual automation editor remain native features.

title: Custom apps: Files and state
text:
## Files and state

```text
/sdcard/Dikciz/apps/<app-id>/
  app.json
  ui.html
  ui.css
  ui.js
  main.js          # main.lua when language is lua
  state.json
  files/          # recordings and other app-owned data
```

`app.json` declares version 1, ID, title, description, language and events. The optional legacy `commands` array is informational metadata and never restricts access. IDs start with a letter and contain up to 64 letters, digits, underscores or hyphens. `imports` and `exports` are reserved. Example:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "id": "example-counter",
  "title": "Event counter",
  "description": "Count custom events without keeping a page open.",
  "language": "javascript",
  "events": ["example.count"]
}
```

Optional `eventSubscriptions` uses the existing [automation subscription format](dikciz-configuration.md#lua-scripts-and-automation), including native source filters and intervals. `events` is shorthand for exact event names with no interval. Optional `locationMonitoring: true` requests a visible location foreground service while timers are pending; it grants no location permission.

State belongs to the exact app ID, independent of page/widget state. Duplicate the bundle with a new manifest ID to get independent state and files. Removing an app deletes its entire public directory. Replacing its bundle preserves state, data and its running or stopped state. Export includes only manifest and source, excluding state, recordings and native execution records. These apps are not currently included in home/chat encrypted backups. Export code and preserve requested data separately.

Source and manifest edits require no permission approval. UI source changes reload the visible app; state-file writes update its live state. Background source loads fresh for the next invocation. Invalid files and subscriptions report validation errors. Stop and Start control background execution, not permissions.

title: Custom apps: Backend
Custom apps: Interface
text:
## Interface

`ui.html`, `ui.css` and `ui.js` use the existing injected `window.dikciz` bridge and app-local command binding. `selfWidget` exposes this app's state and `storagePath`, ending in `/apps/<id>/files`. Its state patch merges top-level fields into app state, preserving unrelated keys and explicit nulls. Use ordinary DOM listeners and await bridge results. An app can call `customAppEvent` to invoke its own backend while its UI is open. Subscribe to `dikciz-state` for persisted state changes and ordinary event callbacks for subscribed native/custom events.

For a complete working reference, read [Travel todo](todo-app-tutorial.md) and its linked source files.

The native manager's **Edit bundle** exposes the complete manifest, HTML, CSS, UI JavaScript and backend source. State can be edited with `customAppState` or the public file. Saving preserves the app's running or stopped state. New apps start enabled. **Start app** and **Disable and stop** control execution without a permission dialog. Opening a stopped app starts it. The native manager is a separate activity, reachable again after Android permission screens take the foreground. Hiding or closing its interface sends `app.ui.hidden` to its backend. Voice notes uses that event to stop its recorder and preserve a pending save for reopening; other apps decide their own hidden behavior.

title: Custom apps: Timers and alerts
text:
## Timers and alerts

`customAppSchedule` schedules a one-shot event with `action: schedule`, `timerId`, `event`, `delayMilliseconds` and optional object `payload`. Delay ranges from 1000 through 604800000 ms. `cancel` selects a timer ID; `cancelAll` selects the app. The host persists timers and owns native wake-up alarms and a visible foreground service. At most 64 timers may be pending across apps; completed history is bounded to 256 records.

Timers are claimed durably before invoking the backend. A handler may reschedule the same ID, which creates a new generation. Pending timers can survive process restart within the same boot. An interrupted claimed timer or a pending timer from another boot becomes `needs_review`; its original effect is not replayed. The host sends `app.resume` with `interrupted: true` for app-defined recovery. Android may delay alarms or reject background starts. Inspect timer state and the latest app run rather than treating scheduling as completed execution.

`customAppAlert` shows an urgent dimmed modal using `action: show`, `episodeId`, `durationMilliseconds`, `title`, `detail`, `cancelLabel` and `cancelEvent`. Duration is 1000 through 3600000 ms. Optional `announcement` and `finalAnnouncement` use `{seconds}`. Only one app can own the urgent alert. Android notification access and an urgent countdown channel are required. Overlay access allows presentation over other apps; otherwise an active Dikciz activity can host a dialog. Keyguard, volume, DND and background restrictions remain Android-controlled. `action: close` releases it.

The modal's cancellation button invokes the app's declared cancel event, then closes. Its native host owns window/audio/vibration cleanup. The app must cancel its pending timers and update its own state. The foreground notification's **Pause apps** invokes `app.stopped`, disables affected apps and cancels pending timers/alerts. For concurrent owner cancellation, `customAppEvent` accepts `interruptRunning: true`, which blocks further mutating calls from the current handler except state and cleanup commands, including geofence deletion. Already submitted effects cannot be recalled.

title: Custom apps: Remote and assistant access
text:
## Remote and assistant access

HTTP, WebSocket and MCP expose the same nine commands: `customAppsList`, `customAppRead`, `customAppInstall`, `customAppControl`, `customAppEvent`, `customAppState`, `customAppSchedule`, `customAppAlert` and `customAppRuntime`. Discover exact fields in the [command reference](command-reference.md). Install/import requires `confirm: true` and starts a new app enabled. Replacing preserves its running or stopped state. Start needs no confirmation; removal retains its destructive-action confirmation. Archives use `.dikciz-app.zip`, exactly five manifest/source entries, no directory entries, no traversal and a 2 MiB compressed-file ceiling. Each source is bounded to 256 KiB; state to 128 KiB and depth 16. At most 64 apps are installed.

These APIs require full owner remote authority. Scoped read grants do not gain execution access. Read-only chat sees only list, read and runtime; the trusted executor rejects hidden mutations even when called directly. Read-only SOS preview also passes its read-only restriction into app command execution and rejects returned actions. Listing or reading records does not invoke source code. `customAppControl: open` reports a request, while `customAppRead.uiVisible` and `snapshot` report observed presentation.

The legacy `sosPlanSave`, `sosPreview`, `sosControl` and `sosStatus` commands delegate to the bundled SOS app. Existing saved plans migrate once into its public state. Active pre-migration runs become `needs_review`, with no automatic outgoing messages. See [SOS setup and outcomes](safety-and-journeys.md).

title: Image recognition dependencies
text:
# Image recognition dependencies

Dikciz source retains its project license. The image-recognition feature additionally bundles Google's ML Kit text-recognition:16.0.1 and barcode-scanning:17.3.0 SDKs, models and their transitive Android dependencies. These are subject to [ML Kit terms and privacy](https://developers.google.com/ml-kit/terms) and incorporated Google API terms. Do not describe the bundled models as GPL source.

Recognition processes image input and results on the device. Google states that the SDK can contact its servers for maintenance information and sends performance/utilization metrics. This is separate from image uploads. Dikciz does not upload images through imageRecognize or documentScan. [Google's installation documentation](https://developers.google.com/ml-kit/tips/installation-paths) describes bundled model behavior.

Pinned direct AAR checksums are verified by the Dikciz Gradle dependency check. Build integration is kept in the flavor dependencies and matching upstream overlay. The optional fixture regeneration command fetches a SHA-pinned MIT-licensed Nayuki QR generator; its source header is retained in the verified cache. Committed PNG fixtures need no generator download during ordinary live tests.

The flavor's ProGuard rules preserve ML Kit registrar constructors referenced through manifest metadata. Run recognition against the minified APK when checking a release; compilation does not exercise registrar loading.

title: Image recognition dependencies: JavaScript interpreter
text:
## JavaScript interpreter

Background scripts bundle Mozilla Rhino 1.9.2 under the [Mozilla Public License 2.0](https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/MPL/2.0/). The unmodified runtime and its source are published by [Mozilla Rhino](https://github.com/mozilla/rhino/releases/tag/Rhino1_9_2_Release). Dikciz pins its version and verifies its JAR checksum in every Dikciz variant. It runs locally in interpreted mode; direct Java class access is disabled.

title: Persistent device connections
text:
# Persistent device connections

Use `deviceConnectionOpen`, then `deviceConnectionExchange`, `deviceConnectionRead` and `deviceConnectionClose`. `deviceConnectionsList` pages lifecycle metadata. These shared commands work through HTTP, WebSocket, MCP, HTML and Lua. Every transfer counts as mutating for token and assistant access control.

Connections retain hardware across commands. The default lifetime is five minutes, configurable with `maximumDurationMilliseconds` from one second to one hour. At most eight connections can be active. A transfer uses `timeoutMilliseconds` (default 30000, maximum 120000), serializes access and closes on timeout. Reads and writes are bounded to 65536 bytes. Closing, expiry or process death releases hardware; retrying an interrupted write can duplicate peer effects. Completed peer effects are not undone.

title: Persistent device connections: Bluetooth
text:
## Bluetooth

`kind: rfcomm` requires a paired device `address` and `serviceUuid`; `secure` defaults true. Exchange writes optional base64 bytes and reads up to `readBytes`. Returned chunks do not promise a complete message. Handle framing in the client.

`kind: gatt` requires an address. Exchange actions are `discover`, `read`, `write`, `subscribe`, `unsubscribe` and `notifications`. Use service/characteristic UUIDs and instance IDs when discovery reports duplicates. Notifications have bounded replay cursors and report loss. Bluetooth access and enabled hardware remain necessary.

The optional **Vehicle console** HTML template uses retained RFCOMM to query an owner-selected ELM327-compatible adapter. It reads RPM, coolant temperature and adapter voltage. It handles command framing and displays observation time. It never clears codes or sends vehicle actuation commands. Add it from the HTML template picker; it is not added to the starter home automatically.

title: Persistent device connections: USB and NFC
text:
## USB and NFC

`kind: usb` requires an attached `deviceId`, optional `interfaceIndex` and owner access. Missing access returns a targeted `usbRequestAccess` recovery. Exchanges support `control`, `bulk` and `interrupt`. Control requires requestType/request/value/index. Bulk and interrupt identify an endpoint on the claimed interface. Supply `readBytes` for input or `dataBase64` for output.

`kind: nfc` requires a foreground unlocked Dikciz activity and a physically presented tag. Choose `technology`, default IsoDep. Supported technologies include NfcA/B/F/V, Ndef and supported Mifare technologies. Exchange supports raw `transceive`, `readNdef` and `writeNdef`. Shared NFC ownership prevents simultaneous one-shot and retained readers. Tag removal is an explicit I/O failure. This does not implement payment decoding or card emulation.

A connected-device foreground notification exposes **Stop all**. Actual profiles, USB endpoints and tag technologies depend on physical hardware. An emulator does not establish real peripheral compatibility.

title: Persistent device connections: Vehicle document
text:
## Vehicle document


This rendered WebView uses a deterministic mocked ELM adapter response with fragmented reads. It verifies framing, PID conversion, saved state and presentation. It is not a photograph of a connected car or proof of physical adapter compatibility.

title: Dikciz configuration
text:
# Dikciz configuration

Dikciz keeps its editable home under `/sdcard/Dikciz/`. The directory is the source of truth for the launcher. Valid changes reload automatically, within a couple of seconds of the write, whether the edit came from the launcher, a script, adb, or a file manager. An invalid file leaves the last accepted home visible and records the failure in the local log.
aliases: settings configuration home workspace grid appearance state files

title: Dikciz configuration: Public file tree
text:
## Public file tree

```text
/sdcard/Dikciz/
├── config.json
├── pages/<page-id>/page.json
├── pages/<page-id>/widgets/<widget-id>.json
├── pages/<page-id>/widgets/<widget-id>/state.json
├── pages/<page-id>/widgets/<widget-id>/items/<instance-id>/state.json
├── pages/<page-id>/widgets/<widget-id>/items/<instance-id>/<custom-file>
├── scripts/<script-id>/script.json
├── scripts/<script-id>/main.lua
├── scripts/<script-id>/main.js
├── scripts/<script-id>/state.json
├── scripts/<script-id>/run-status.json
├── scripts/imports/
├── scripts/exports/
├── apps/<app-id>/app.json
├── apps/<app-id>/ui.html
├── apps/<app-id>/ui.css
├── apps/<app-id>/ui.js
├── apps/<app-id>/main.js
├── apps/<app-id>/state.json
├── apps/<app-id>/files/
├── widget-library/<package-id>/widget.json
├── widget-library/<package-id>/index.html
├── widget-library/<package-id>/style.css
├── widget-library/<package-id>/script.js
├── automation/policies/<policy-id>.json
├── automation/scripts/<script-id>.json
├── control/remote-auth.json
├── control/ports.json
├── themes/<theme-id>.json
├── fonts/
├── wallpapers/
└── logs/YYYY-MM-DD.log
```

On first run, Android must grant Dikciz access to this directory. The storage screen links to Android's own access panel. Until Android grants it, the control planes still expose the storage screen for inspection but cannot load or change configuration.

Each file has one job. `config.json` owns global settings and the home manifest. Pages own their metadata and widget references. Widgets, scripts, automation rules, themes, and library packages remain separate so a normal edit does not turn the root into one large document.

The bundled [Travel todo](todo-app-tutorial.md) is a source-linked example of app state and native-event wiring.

[Custom apps](custom-apps.md) live independently of `configGet` and page/widget configuration. Their manifest chooses `main.js` or `main.lua` and event subscriptions. All apps share the Android access granted to Dikciz. UI edits reload that app; state updates reach its active WebView and backend source loads on invocation. Manifest edits require no permission approval and preserve running/stopped state. Existing edited bundles survive updates. Their data and source are excluded from current encrypted home/chat backups.
aliases: settings configuration home workspace grid appearance state files

title: Dikciz configuration: Edit and inspect configuration
text:
## Edit and inspect configuration

Use Android file tools, an ADB tunnel, or the control planes. In the lab, move only an artifact through the provided targets:

```bash
DEVICE_FILE=/sdcard/Dikciz/config.json ARTIFACT_FILE=config.json make adb-pull
# Edit .android-lab/shared/artifacts/config.json.
DEVICE_FILE=/sdcard/Dikciz/config.json ARTIFACT_FILE=config.json make adb-push
```

The control planes expose a complete assembled document. They validate a full replacement atomically, write the matching public tree, and reload the home:

| Interface | Read | Replace | Restore bundled home |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| WebSocket | `configGet` | `configReplace` or `configSeed` | `reset` |
| MCP | `dikciz_config_get` | `dikciz_config_replace` or `dikciz_config_seed` | `dikciz_config_reset` |

`configReplace` is a complete replacement, never a partial patch. Start by reading `configGet`, edit the returned document, then replace it. The command result contains the normalized saved configuration and a fresh semantic UI snapshot.
aliases: settings configuration home workspace grid appearance state files

title: Dikciz configuration: Root document
text:
## Root document

`config.json` has a version and Dikciz-owned namespaces:

```json
{
  "version": 4,
  "limits": {
    "maxConfigBytes": 1048576,
    "maxComponentCharacters": 512,
    "maxHtmlWidgetDocumentBytes": 196608,
    "maxHtmlWidgetsPerPage": 8,
    "maxIdentifierCharacters": 80,
    "maxPages": 24,
    "maxTextCharacters": 65536,
    "maxTitleCharacters": 120,
    "maxWidgetsPerPage": 128
  },
  "logging": { "level": "info", "retentionDays": 7, "maxTotalBytes": 16777216 },
  "launcher": {
    "home": {
      "homePageId": "home",
      "selectedPageId": "home",
      "selectedThemeId": "dikciz-dark",
      "styleDefaults": { "widget": {} },
      "pages": ["home"]
    }
  }
}
```

The assembled view returned by `configGet` also contains scripts and automation objects. The persisted tree keeps their named source and policy files separate. Dikciz preserves root namespaces and sibling objects under `launcher` that it does not own when it performs a native edit. Version 4 is required; older documents are rejected rather than migrated.

`limits` bounds document size, identifiers, titles, page count, widgets per page, component strings, and HTML renderer resources. The bundled limits are a one MiB configuration, 24 pages, 128 widgets per page, 65,536 text characters, 120-character titles, and 80-character identifiers. `maxHtmlWidgetsPerPage` defaults to eight enabled HTML widgets. Native shortcuts, app groups, provider widgets, and the native script dashboard do not consume that budget. `maxHtmlWidgetDocumentBytes` defaults to 196,608 UTF-8 bytes for the fully generated HTML document, including the widget context Dikciz injects at load time. The parser also applies non-configurable upper limits before reading a file.

`logging` controls level, retained days, disk budget, failed-script notifications, and the notification quiet period. See [Logs](#logs).
aliases: settings configuration home workspace grid appearance state files

title: Dikciz configuration: Pages and widget files
text:
## Pages and widget files

A page has a stable ID, title, two-axis position, lock state, and widget IDs:

```json
{
  "id": "home",
  "title": "Home",
  "position": { "column": 0, "row": 0 },
  "locked": false,
  "widgets": ["command-deck"]
}
```

Page positions are zero-based in files. Human-facing addresses are one-based: `1H1V` is column one, row one. A widget's complete address combines that page address and widget ID, for example `1H1V-command-deck`. The address changes when a widget moves to another page. Its ID does not.

Long press the empty part of a page rail, past its dots, to create a page. The new page lands at the far end of that rail, never beside the page you are on. Holding the horizontal rail before the dots inserts a new first column and shifts every existing column right; holding it after the dots appends a new last column. The vertical rail does the same at the top and the bottom of the current column. The page is saved and selected immediately, so there is nothing to confirm and nothing to lose by navigating away.

Reorder pages from the page menu under **Move this page**: **Move left**, **Move right**, **Move up**, and **Move down**. Each one exchanges this page's coordinate with the single page already sitting at the neighbouring coordinate. A direction with no page there is shown disabled and changes nothing. A move rewrites only `position`, so page IDs, titles, locks, widgets, `homePageId`, and `selectedPageId` all survive it. A locked page can neither create a page nor be moved.

Every widget has `id`, `type`, `enabled`, `cell`, `locked`, and optional `style`. Visible cards also have `title`. IDs are global and case-insensitively unique across all pages. Native creation makes readable lowercase slugs with a numeric suffix. Widgets never stack. `zIndex` is not a supported widget key, and Dikciz rejects a configuration that contains it.

Supported widget types are:

| Type | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `html` | A resizable WebView with local HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and state. |
| `app` | One explicit Android activity shortcut. |
| `appGroup` | A native group of up to 32 Android activity components, made by dropping one app tile onto another. |
| `provider` | A native third-party Android AppWidget provider card. |
| `scriptDashboard` | Native view for script state, logs, enablement, and editing. |

`text`, `toggle`, and `lua` are not widget types. Create visible controls as HTML widgets. Lua stays in the script tree and appears in a script dashboard.
aliases: settings configuration home workspace grid appearance state files

title: Dikciz configuration: The native page grid
text:
### The native page grid

A native page is one fixed viewport. It never gains canvas height, and adding a widget never scrolls the page below an existing widget.

`launcher.home.nativeGrid` describes the grid every page is laid out on:

```json
{ "nativeGrid": { "columns": 8, "rows": 6, "gapDp": 8, "outerPaddingDp": 12 } }
```

`columns` and `rows` accept 1 to 12. `gapDp` and `outerPaddingDp` accept 0 to
64. The bundled default is 8 columns by 6 rows. The record is optional; a
document without it uses that default.

The right and bottom pager rails provide the trailing outer spacing. The page renderer applies `outerPaddingDp` at the left and top without adding it again beside those rails. Widget style margins remain additional spacing. Explicit saved grid dimensions remain unchanged on update.

Every top-level widget owns whole grid cells through one `cell` record:

```json
{ "cell": { "column": 0, "row": 0, "columnSpan": 2, "rowSpan": 1 } }
```

`column` and `row` are zero-based cell indexes. Both spans are cell counts and are at least 1. The rectangle must fit inside the configured grid, and two widgets on one page may never claim the same cell. Rendered pixels are derived from the current viewport at draw time, so the same logical rectangle survives page selection, process recreation, and rotation.

`cell` is the only placement a widget carries. Any other placement key is an unknown key and the strict parser rejects the document.
aliases: settings configuration home workspace grid appearance state files

title: Dikciz configuration: Placement failures
text:
### Placement failures

Dropping a widget on a cell another widget already holds is not always a failure. The tile under the pointer decides what the drop means:

- two app tiles merge into one `appGroup`, and an app tile dropped on a group joins it;
- two widgets that cover the same number of cells trade places;
- anything else is refused.

Both outcomes are shown while the finger is still down. A merge target swells, and a trade moves both tiles at once, so leaving the cell puts the other widget back before the drop.

Placement reports one of three finite failures. A rejected operation writes nothing to the public tree and emits one bounded diagnostic.

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `page_full` | The page has no free cell for any further item. |
| `grid_collision` | The requested cells are already used. |
| `grid_bounds` | The rectangle leaves the configured grid. |
aliases: settings configuration home workspace grid appearance state files

title: Dikciz configuration: Editing the page grid
text:
### Editing the page grid

The grid is editable in **Settings**, under **Page grid**, and through the `gridSet` command and the `dikciz_grid_set` tool. One grid applies to every page.

Changing dimensions reflows every page, including locked and unselected pages. Shrinking scales widget edges to the smaller grid, with at least one cell per axis. Full-width and full-height widgets follow the corresponding grid dimension when it grows too. Items are processed in saved order; a collision uses the first free rectangle of the adjusted size. An item with no fitting space is removed from the page. Removing an app shortcut leaves its app installed; removing a widget also removes its scoped state. The new grid and adjusted pages are saved together. Spacing-only changes preserve placements.

While a widget is being moved or resized, the page draws every cell of the grid behind the content. Placement snaps to whole cells, so the guides show where the widget can land. They appear when a move is armed or a resize starts, and they go away when the gesture ends.

Direct configuration replacement remains strict: each widget must carry a valid `cell` record. Use Settings or `gridSet` to reflow an existing layout. Omitting `nativeGrid` uses the bundled grid; it does not make legacy pixel placement valid.
aliases: settings configuration home workspace grid appearance state files

title: Dikciz configuration: Native app shortcuts and app drawer
text:
## Native app shortcuts and app drawer

The Dikciz mark beside the horizontal page rail opens the launcher controls, and from there the native app drawer. An upward swipe that starts on that rail opens it too. Search filters launchable installed apps by label or package name. Tap a result to launch it. Use its overflow button, or long press the row, for add shortcut, Android app info, uninstall, and force stop.

Android owns the confirmation for app info and uninstall. Force stop requests root and reports `root_unavailable` when `su` is unavailable or denied. It never falls back to the ordinary Dikciz app shell.

Adding an app places an `app` tile in the first free grid cell, row-major from the top left. A page with no free cell rejects the request with `page_full` and adds nothing. The placed tile is left selected so its move and resize controls work straight away. A tap anywhere on the tile launches the activity, and a drag from anywhere on it moves the tile to another free rectangle. A widget that owns its own content, an HTML document, an Android provider view, or the script dashboard, is dragged from its top `24Dp` instead, because its body needs the touches for itself.

An app tile draws its icon as the largest square the cell allows, measured against the narrower side, with the icon and its label centred in the cell as a pair. Resizing the tile resizes the icon with it.

Dropping one app tile onto another makes an `appGroup` holding both, in drop order, at the target's cell. The group opens as a grid of its member icons. A tap launches a member and a long press removes it. Removing down to a single member replaces the group with a plain `app` widget for the survivor, keeping the cell and the widget ID, so a script addressing that widget keeps working. A group is never saved with fewer than two members.

An `app` widget stores one flattened Android `component` and one `displayStyle`:

| `displayStyle` | Appearance |
| --- | --- |
| `iconLabel` | App icon and label. This is the default. |
| `button` | Text button. |
| `buttonIconLabel` | Button with icon and label. |

The native drawer and the `appCatalogue` and `appAction` commands share the same installed-app catalogue and action runtime. Command calls use a flattened component. `addShortcut` needs a selected native page and is rejected from Lua's returned typed actions, which have no selected-page context. Lua owner command calls use the serving launcher's selected page.

title: Dikciz configuration: HTML widgets
text:
## HTML widgets

The assembled HTML widget record returned by `configGet` is a normal, resizable home widget:

```json
{
  "id": "device-card",
  "type": "html",
  "title": "Device card",
  "html": "<main><output id=\"status\">Loading</output></main>",
  "css": "main { padding: 16px; color: white; }",
  "javascript": "window.addEventListener('dikciz-ready', () => {});",
  "state": { "status": "ready" },
  "heightMode": "content",
  "enabled": true,
  "cell": { "column": 0, "row": 0, "columnSpan": 2, "rowSpan": 2 }
}
```

`heightMode` is `fixed` when omitted. `content` fits the rendered document inside the widget's assigned row span without expanding its cells or the page. Long press the move handle, content or background for the same whole-widget edit, appearance, resize, fit-content, lock and delete actions. Edit exposes HTML, CSS, JavaScript and JSON state together. HTML elements and `data-*` attributes are document content, not native preset objects. Page and widget locks protect editing. Dikciz consumes long presses so the WebView does not start browser text selection or browser controls.

HTML widgets hide native and CSS scrollbars, including those in nested scroll containers. Touch, keyboard and programmatic scrolling still work. In **Appearance**, set **Border / Widths / All sides** to `0` to remove the native outline (`style.border.widths.all: 0`). Set individual side widths to `0` too if the widget or theme supplies them; individual widths take precedence over `all`. Borders drawn by the HTML itself are controlled by its CSS.

The native WebView viewport is clipped to the widget frame even when document CSS overflows. During resize, Dikciz draws the native outline and handles over the WebView, so the frame stays visible and remains the resize boundary.

The public widget descriptor `<widget-id>.json` stores source and layout. Wrapper `state` is stored separately in `<widget-id>/state.json`. Card `itemStates` are split into `<widget-id>/items/<instance-id>/state.json`, under that widget's page directory. `configGet` and `widgetGet` assemble those values into the same record. Legacy state embedded in a widget descriptor migrates after the complete configuration passes validation.

JSON state patches preserve null values in objects and arrays; null does not remove a key.

State changes do not reload the WebView. The document receives `dikciz-state`, and `selfWidget.state` becomes the full replacement state. Update only the DOM nodes that changed.

The native editor is a source editor, not an HTML preview. Its labeled `HTML`, `CSS`, and `JavaScript` fields use code text and a boxed editor frame. They show literal source, including tags, comments, and entities. For example, a divider is shown as `<hr class="dikciz-block dikciz-block-divider" />`, not as a rendered rule. Opening **Edit HTML widget** always reads the current saved widget record, including source changed after the long-press menu opened.

HTML packages are reusable starters under `widget-library/<package-id>/`. A package has strict metadata in `widget.json`, `index.html`, and optional `style.css` and `script.js`. `widget.json` is at version 2 and declares a `span` with `columnSpan` and `rowSpan` instead of a pixel `size`. The Dikciz category lists packages directly with searchable titles and descriptions. Selecting one opens its preview; Load copies its source into a new sibling widget placed on the grid. Empty HTML widget inserts a blank document without a library submenu. Choosing a package never edits an existing widget's source. Later package changes do not silently modify placed widgets. Save an edited widget to make or replace a package. Dikciz stages and validates a complete replacement before it publishes it. If a save is interrupted, the next library read either completes a valid retained stage or restores the last valid package. The picker never shows a partial package.

title: Dikciz configuration: Complete WebView templates
text:
### Complete WebView templates

The library contains whole documents: `time-weather`, `most-used-apps`, `agenda`, `voice-notes`, `device-status`, `home-dashboard`, `command-deck`, `quick-apps`, `quick-note`, `system-dashboard`, `sensors-dashboard`, `markets-news`, `app-launcher`, `brightness`, `lock-screen`, `notifications` and `system-status`. Each placed widget owns its full HTML, CSS, JavaScript and state. Library source is copied at insertion; there are no native card preset objects or fragment picker. Ordinary DOM sections remain programmable through the document's own JavaScript.

The device and system templates draw a battery ring, RAM/storage bars, bounded process CPU history and per-core tiles from `deviceState`. Process CPU uses the available-processor capacity scale. System/per-core load and clock frequencies appear only where Android exposes them; protected values stay unknown and cannot be unlocked by a runtime permission. Effects respect reduced motion and visibility. Sensor inventory lists hardware, not live readings. The market template uses explicit Coinbase and GDELT requests and retains dated results in its widget state. See [starter templates](starter-home.md#optional-complete-templates) for sources and refresh behavior.

Dikciz installs a bundled package only when that package ID has no public directory yet. It never overwrites an existing package during an app update, so a user-edited starter remains the user's version. Save an edited widget to replace that package deliberately, or delete that one package directory before the next fresh installation if the bundled version is wanted again.

The JavaScript bridge and event model are documented in [Automation control](automation-control.md#html-widget-javascript).

title: Dikciz configuration: Lua scripts and automation
text:
## Lua scripts and automation

Lua and JavaScript scripts are background or event-driven logic. Metadata accepts optional `language`, either `lua` (the default) or `javascript`. JavaScript uses `main.js`; Lua uses `main.lua`. The [background JavaScript guide](background-javascript.md) covers its handler and shared contracts. Each script has four files:

```text
scripts/<script-id>/script.json      metadata and enabled state
scripts/<script-id>/main.lua         source
scripts/<script-id>/state.json       explicit script input and saved state
scripts/<script-id>/run-status.json  latest result written by Dikciz
```

Each enabled script requires a referenced automation policy and subscription:

```json
{
  "id": "status",
  "title": "Status automation",
  "enabled": true,
  "capabilities": ["battery", "locationPrecise"],
  "actions": ["patchState", "patchWidget", "postNotification"]
}
```

`capabilities` names the events the script may receive. `actions` names the typed actions it may return, and Dikciz enforces that list when the action runs. Enabled scripts also have owner command access through `context.request` and `context.requestJson`; this command access is not restricted by the returned-action list. An action a script returns that its policy does not list is refused with the outcome `capability_denied`, the launcher does nothing, and the refusal is logged with that `reason`. A script whose policy is missing gets no actions at all. Actions a Dikciz HTML widget dispatches directly are not policy gated, because the owner invokes those on the device.

```json
{
  "scriptId": "status",
  "policyId": "status",
  "enabled": true,
  "subscriptions": [
    {
      "event": "battery",
      "minimumIntervalMilliseconds": 60000,
      "coalescingKey": "battery-status"
    }
  ]
}
```

The current capability names are:

```text
time, battery, charging, powerSaveState, deviceIdleState, nightModeState,
deviceConfiguration, appPackagesMetadata, ringerModeState,
interruptionFilterState, connectivity, thermalState, bluetoothState, screen,
userPresence, alarm, sensors, healthSteps, locationApproximate,
locationPrecise, calendarEventsMetadata, calendarEventsContent,
contactsMetadata, phoneState, smsMetadata, smsContent, notificationsMetadata,
notificationsContent, mediaSessionsMetadata, mediaSessionsContent,
clipboardMetadata, clipboardContent, widgetState, deviceAdministration,
manualTrigger, accessibility
```

The current policy action capability names are:

```text
accessibilityAction, accessibilityGesture, accessibilityGlobalAction,
selectPage, patchWidget, patchState, patchDom, launchApp, appAction,
postNotification, sendSms, explicitIntent, emitEvent, mediaControl,
mediaVolume, notificationControl, lockDevice
```

The list above contains policy capability names. The volume action record uses `type: "setMediaVolume"` and integer `levelPercent` from 0 through 100, while its policy allows `mediaVolume`. See the [complete typed action reference](typed-actions.md) for fields and policy mappings.

Read the [scripting tutorial](scripting-tutorial.md) for end-to-end event subscriptions, custom events, HTML bridge calls, cross-widget state, and action results.

`sendSms` takes a `recipient` and a `body`. The recipient is a dialable number of up to 20 characters: digits with an optional leading `+` and the usual dialling punctuation. The body uses the configured text limit and is divided into parts when it is longer than one message segment.

Dikciz does not request the default SMS role. It does not directly insert sent messages into Android's SMS provider, but Android can persist messages sent by non-default SMS apps, so they can appear in the owner's messaging history. See [Android's SMS provider behavior](https://android-developers.googleblog.com/2013/10/getting-your-sms-apps-ready-for-kitkat.html). Android can rate-limit sends or ask the owner for confirmation. The limits depend on the device. Dikciz reports what Android returned and does not work around that prompt.

The action needs the `SEND_SMS` Android permission, which `automationStatus` reports as `smsSend` under `androidAccess`. Without it the action returns `android_permission_denied` and sends nothing. A policy that does not declare `sendSms` is refused before Android is reached.

Event subscriptions use the published event names: `time`, `battery`, `charging`, `powerSaveMode`, `deviceIdleMode`, `nightMode`, `deviceConfiguration`, `packageChanged`, `ringerMode`, `interruptionFilter`, `connectivity`, `thermalStatus`, `bluetoothState`, `screen`, `userPresent`, `alarm`, `sensor`, `healthDailySteps`, `location`, `calendarEvent`, `contactsChanged`, `phoneState`, `smsReceived`, `notificationPosted`, `notificationRemoved`, `mediaSession`, `clipboardChanged`, `widgetChanged`, `deviceAdminState`, `accessibilityWindow`, `accessibilityServiceState`, and `manual`.

Use a new valid event name for a custom event, for example:

```json
{
  "event": "weather.refresh.completed",
  "minimumIntervalMilliseconds": 0
}
```

Both Lua and HTML can emit it. Subscribers receive the name in `event.type` and the JSON object in `event.payload`.

`minimumIntervalMilliseconds` is a per-script-subscription monotonic delivery floor. It suppresses a matching event when that subscription was delivered too recently. Alarm subscriptions also keep their own due time: Dikciz wakes at the shortest active alarm interval, but a longer subscription runs only when its own deadline is due. A configuration replacement begins a new schedule window. After a process restart, the retained Android alarm causes one recovery delivery and starts the next deadline from that delivery. Late alarms run once and move their next due time ahead from that delivery. Dikciz does not replay missed intervals in a burst. Turning off either the script or its automation entry stops its Android sources and cancels its alarm schedule.

A `location` subscription needs `locationPrecision`, either `approximate` or `precise`, and the value decides both the capability it needs and what the event carries. A precise subscription needs `locationPrecise` and the Android fine-location permission, and its payload carries `provider`, `latitude`, `longitude`, `accuracy`, `altitude`, `bearing`, and `speed`. An approximate subscription needs `locationApproximate` and either Android location permission, and its payload carries only `provider` and a `latitude` and `longitude` rounded to two decimal places, about a kilometre. Dikciz reads the device location once and then builds one event per subscribed precision, so an approximate subscription receives the approximate event even while the launcher holds the fine permission for some other subscription. A precise subscription without the fine permission registers nothing and receives nothing.

Lua receives a bounded event table plus read-only `context.state`, `context.widgets`, and `context.androidAccess`. The last object is the same current Android access map that `automationStatus.androidAccess` returns. It contains Booleans only, not Android object handles. During `accessibilityWindow`, Lua also receives the bounded active Android tree in `context.accessibility`. Return a status and actions. `accessibilityServiceState` has only its fixed event payload: `state` is `connected`, `interrupted`, or `disconnected`, and `enabled` is the current Accessibility owner-setting Boolean. It does not include `context.accessibility` because it has no active-window snapshot. `accessibilityAction` requires its current `snapshotId`, a generated `nodeId`, and a supported action. `accessibilityGesture` uses its current `snapshotId` with a bounded `tap` or `swipe` document. `accessibilityGlobalAction` uses one supported Android global action name. `patchWidget` targets a complete widget address such as `1H1V-command-deck`. Enabled scripts can use `context.request` or `context.requestJson` for ordinary launcher commands, including shell, files, intents and semantic UI input, with the same validation and Android access checks as the local control planes. These functions accept JSON strings or object tables and return canonical result/error responses. Lua receives no Android object handles. See the [Lua command reference](scripting-tutorial.md#return-device-and-launcher-actions-from-lua).

title: Dikciz configuration: Lua runtime surface
text:
### Lua runtime surface

The [scripting tutorial](scripting-tutorial.md) documents the supported runtime surface. Core globals are `assert`, `error`, `ipairs`, `next`, `pairs`, `pcall`, `select`, `tonumber`, `tostring`, `type`, and `xpcall`. Available libraries are `math`, `string`, `table`, and `bit32`.

The runtime removes dynamic loading and host escape routes: `debug`, `io`, `os`, `package`, `require`, `load`, `dofile`, `loadfile`, and `print` are not available. It also removes `string.format`, `string.gsub`, `string.rep`, `table.concat`, `table.move`, and `table.unpack` to keep script work bounded. Scripts receive no Android object handles. Use the typed action list above or the owner command functions for launcher and Android behavior.

Fresh Dikciz includes six disabled example scripts, including the three Goblin GPS/weather demonstrations described in the [starter catalog](starter-home.md#optional-lua-utilities). Their enabled policies and subscriptions become active only after the owner enables the corresponding Lua source record.

| Script | What it does after enabling |
| --- | --- |
| `low-battery` | Notifies once at 20 percent or lower while discharging. Charging or reaching 30 percent resets the reminder. |
| `charge-ready` | Notifies once at 80 percent or higher while charging. Unplugging or dropping below 75 percent resets it. |
| `screen-lock` | Locks only when explicitly run, after checking Device Administration. It never runs when access changes. |
| `goblin-london` | Speaks on entry into its central-London radius, with precise GPS accuracy checks, exit rearming and a six-hour cooldown. |
| `goblin-heat` | Speaks above 35 Celsius from fresh outdoor-weather events, rearms below 32 Celsius and uses a 30-minute cooldown. |
| `goblin-speed` | Speaks above 80 km/h from accurate precise GPS speed, rearms below 65 km/h and uses a 15-minute cooldown. |

The Goblin London and speed examples subscribe to precise location only after their Lua source is enabled. Goblin heat consumes `goblin.weather` events emitted by the visible Goblin widget. The [starter home guide](starter-home.md) covers all four pages, every bundled template and script, weather data sources, permissions, cooldowns and customization.

Use the native Script dashboard or Settings to enable, disable, edit, import, export, delete, inspect status, and read logs. The dashboard, Settings, WebSocket `scriptLogs`, and MCP `dikciz_script_logs` read the same safe log projection. A failed Lua compile or handler run keeps `invalid_lua` as its stable run status. Its matching log record includes a bounded, sanitized `diagnostic` with the public `scripts/<script-id>/main.lua` location and line when LuaJ provides one. Credential-shaped values are redacted before the native viewer or either remote control plane receives the record.

title: Dikciz configuration: Android access
text:
## Android access

The Dikciz manifest declares a broad Android access surface. It includes location, contacts, calendar, phone and call state, SMS, camera, microphone, Bluetooth, nearby Wi-Fi, media, notifications, activity and body sensors, Health Connect, files, exact alarms, overlays, writable system settings, usage access, package installation, battery-optimization exemption, Device Administration, and notification-listener support.

The declaration allows Dikciz to request access. Android, the installer, the selected device role, the OEM, and root manager still decide whether it is available. Enable the automation policy first, then use **Settings**, then **Automation**, then **Set up full device access**. Setup opens a separate **Full device access** task in Recents. Its checklist refreshes when you return from an Android access panel or another app, including after activity recreation. Closing it removes the setup task. Each missing access has its own button, and the next setup button follows current Android grants. `automationStatus` and `dikciz_automation_status` return the same machine-readable status.

The `deviceAccess` inventory includes the `sms` runtime-permission entry for reading, receiving and sending SMS. It does not include a default SMS role or request replacing the default messaging app.

Cross-app Android UI automation is an Accessibility service requirement. Its record is `deviceAccess.requirements[id="accessibility"]`; its current Boolean is `automationStatus.androidAccess.accessibility`. The state is `needsSetup` until the phone owner enables Dikciz in Android's Accessibility settings, then becomes `granted`. This is not a runtime permission and is not configurable in `config.json`, a Lua policy, an HTML widget, WebSocket, or MCP. Those surfaces can inspect the state and open the Android panel only.

The local `shell` command and `dikciz_shell` tool request `su` by default. Dikciz first runs `su -c id -u`; only an exact UID of `0` permits the requested command and `executionScope: "root"`. A missing, denied, malformed, or timed out root probe returns `root_unavailable` through WebSocket and an MCP tool error. It never falls back to Dikciz's app user. Pass `root: false` for the ordinary `/system/bin/sh` route, whose result reports `executionScope: "app_sandbox"`, exit code, output, and truncation state.

title: Dikciz configuration: Remote bearer authentication
text:
## Remote bearer authentication

`control/remote-auth.json` is separate from `config.json`. It stores the owner bcrypt verifier, cost and enabled state. Named-token records add bounded metadata, grant lists and generated-token SHA-256 digests. Plaintext credentials are never stored. Password-only records retain their existing format. Set, replace, clear, enable, or disable the password from **Settings**, then **Automation**. The phone does not ask for the old password when changing it.

Create named credentials through **Manage access tokens**; see [token grants and administration](remote-access-tokens.md). Revoke every token before clearing or disabling authentication. When enabled, HTTP, WebSocket and MCP requests on every interface need `Authorization: Bearer <password-or-token>`. A remote client can check, enable, or disable the setting with the documented remote-auth commands. The remote-auth commands cannot retrieve, replace or clear the password. File APIs deny the verifier and its atomic aliases, but an independently authorized app-UID/root shell is not restricted by those file-command guards; see [Android access](android-access.md#credentials-and-privilege-limits). Enabling or disabling remotely requires an owner credential even while authentication is disabled. An invalid auth record refuses connections until repaired or cleared on the phone.
aliases: settings configuration home workspace grid appearance state files

title: Dikciz configuration: Control ports
text:
## Control ports

`control/ports.json` sets the listen address and ports of both listeners. Plain HTTP JSON commands share `mcpPort` at `/v1/automation`; MCP uses `/mcp` on that port. Both use the same bearer and Origin checks. The [files, APKs and shell guide](files-and-apks.md) documents HTTP requests.

Example:

```json
{ "version": 1, "listenAddress": "0.0.0.0", "websocketPort": 19001, "mcpPort": 19002 }
```

Change them in **Settings**, then **Automation**, then **Configure control ports**. Saving a changed address or port restarts both listeners and closes their open connections. **Reset to defaults** deletes the file. Direct file edits also apply automatically, including atomic file replacements and writes through ADB. The configuration watcher restarts both listeners when their address or ports change, without restarting the launcher or rebuilding the home. Rewriting the same endpoints keeps existing connections open. Deleting the file restores the defaults.

`listenAddress` is an optional numeric IPv4 or IPv6 address. It defaults to `127.0.0.1` for existing records. Set it to `0.0.0.0` to accept connections on all IPv4 interfaces, including Wi-Fi and a reachable VPN interface, or choose a specific local interface address. Hostnames, empty values and malformed addresses are rejected. Network binding preserves the existing bearer authentication and browser Origin checks.

Ports must be whole numbers from 1024 to 65535 and must differ. Without the file, Dikciz uses `127.0.0.1` on ports 19001 and 19002. If the file is invalid, Dikciz logs `control_ports_invalid`, uses the defaults and says so in Settings, and reports the fallback in its status. A port conflict can still prevent a listener from starting. There is no dedicated command for changing listener settings. `controlStatus` reports each listener's `listenAddress` and `port` under `transports`.

For direct access, connect to the phone's reachable private hostname or IP and the configured device ports. Enable bearer authentication and allow computer-to-phone traffic in the network policy. `0.0.0.0` is a binding value, not a client destination; it also accepts reachable Wi-Fi clients. Follow [Connect without USB](automation-control.md#connect-without-usb) for setup and troubleshooting.

If using ADB forwarding, update the mappings after a port change, for example `make forward ANDROID_LAB_FORWARD_DEVICE_PORT=<websocket-port> ANDROID_LAB_MCP_DEVICE_PORT=<mcp-port>`.

title: Dikciz configuration: Themes and fonts
text:
## Themes and fonts

`launcher.home.selectedThemeId` selects a reusable JSON file under `themes/`. Theme data is never copied into every widget. The selected theme supplies the base widget style, `styleDefaults.widget` overrides it, and a widget's `style` object overrides individual background, border, spacing, text, and font fields. Applying a theme from the picker clears the launcher background override, style defaults, and widget style overrides; later appearance edits mark the theme as modified. A missing selected theme is reported as missing.

Fonts can be bundled, Android system choices, or a plain `.ttf`, `.otf`, or `.ttc` filename in `fonts/`. Wallpapers are PNG, JPEG, or WebP files in `wallpapers/`.

title: Dikciz configuration: Logs
text:
## Logs

Dikciz writes JSON Lines diagnostics under `/sdcard/Dikciz/logs/YYYY-MM-DD.log`, with UTC dates in filenames and complete UTC timestamps in each record. Open **Settings**, **Configure logging** to choose the minimum level (`debug`, `info`, `warn` or `error`) and retention from 1 to 90 days. Saving applies immediately; Cancel does not change configuration. DEBUG includes all levels; INFO includes INFO, WARN and ERROR. Native edits preserve the other logging values. Existing file-based logging edits also reload automatically. Defaults are INFO, seven days and a 16 MiB cleanup budget. Cleanup removes older daily files; the active UTC day's file stays even if it exceeds the budget. The logging object can enable failed-script Android notifications and set the minimum interval for each script's failure alert. HTML widget console warnings and errors are included as HTML-kind records with the stable widget ID. Assignment-shaped credentials and bearer values in console text are redacted before persistence. If an Android WebView renderer is lost, Dikciz destroys and recreates only that widget in its existing native frame. The Settings viewer and control planes return a bounded safe record list, including launcher-component records that use their component name in the record's script-ID field for compatibility. App-action records retain the action and target as `actionType` and nullable `componentPackage` in the viewer and both control planes. The raw files use `action` and `component_package`. Successful app launches remain logged without a success popup. They do not return raw script source, state, widget text, or configuration.

title: Dikciz configuration: Recovery
text:
## Recovery

**Reset Dikciz home** restores the bundled home, grid, validation limits, scripts, policies, and subscriptions. It keeps other root namespaces and unrelated Android launcher data. It removes obsolete Dikciz AppWidget allocations.

**Safe mode** starts the bundled first page without writing the current public configuration. It keeps read-only file browsing and downloads, install-status queries, diagnostics, snapshots, logs, screenshot, UI dump, reset, and normal-restart recovery paths available while it blocks normal home edits and device mutation commands.

title: Dikciz configuration: Source map
text:
## Source map

The [Dikciz source map](../app/src/dikciz/README.md) identifies the configuration store, style codec, theme loader, widget libraries, and automation runtime that implement this contract.
